modules.outcome: After this part you can choose one ordinary work example and describe, from the person's side, what they need to be able to do with it.

recall.question: In part 1, what did the lesson ask you to describe first about your work example?

options.text: The organization's purpose and, separately, what the person receiving it needs to be able to do.
options.feedback: Right. Those are two different questions. The purpose might be to schedule a meeting; the person's task is to understand why it matters, weigh choices, arrange support and respond.

options.text: Every culture and language of the people you serve.
options.feedback: The lesson said you do not need to know every culture to begin. Start with one example and the person's task, then ask respectfully.

options.text: Who exactly did not respond to it, and why.
options.feedback: Learning notes stay free of personal details, and the lesson says a response pattern does not tell you why anyone did not respond. Describe the task and intended experience instead.

recall.question: Several people have not responded to the sample notice. Which starting point did part 1 recommend?

options.text: Send the same notice more often until responses improve.
options.feedback: Repeating an unclear message can repeat the same barrier. Understand the experience first; a reminder may come later.

options.text: Examine how people receive, understand and use the notice, without assuming why anyone did not respond.
options.feedback: Yes. A reasonable inquiry comes first, then an appropriate change, then a check on what happened.

options.text: Treat the silence as a sign that people are not interested.
options.feedback: A response pattern does not tell you anyone's motivation. Language, format, timing or delivery could all be involved.

decisions.scenario: You are starting the curriculum and need to pick a work example to examine across the nine parts.
decisions.question: Which example do you choose?

options.text: A routine public notice, form or instruction you work with, described in general terms.
options.feedback: Good choice. The lesson asks for one ordinary part of your work that you can examine safely, and you can change it later.

options.text: A sensitive situation you handled recently, with the details that make it real.
options.feedback: Keep names, health information and other private details out of learning notes. A general, non-sensitive example works better and is safer.

options.text: Nothing yet, until you are sure you have authority to change it.
options.feedback: You do not need authority over a whole program to begin. Pick something ordinary; part 5 covers what you can change and who approves.

decisions.scenario: A colleague has drafted a notice and asks you to look it over before it goes out. They say it is accurate and went out on time last year.
decisions.question: What do you look at first?

options.text: Whether the notice went out on schedule and reached the right addresses.
options.feedback: Delivery matters, but the lesson's focus is the person's experience. A letter can be accurate and on time and still be hard to use.

options.text: What the person receiving it needs to understand and do, and whether the notice supports that.
options.feedback: Yes. Standard 1 is about services people can understand and use, not only whether information was sent.

options.text: Whether the wording matches what the team has always used.
options.feedback: Familiar wording feels clear to the people who use it daily. Check whether someone meeting it for the first time can understand the purpose and the next step.

decisions.scenario: In a team discussion about low responses, one colleague wants to learn how people actually experience the notice. Another says that will delay action for months.
decisions.question: How do you respond?

options.text: Agree to wait until the team has complete information before changing anything.
options.feedback: The lesson does not ask for perfect information. It asks for a reasonable inquiry, an appropriate change and a check on what happened.

options.text: Suggest a reasonable inquiry now, then try an appropriate change and check what happened.
options.feedback: Right. Understanding the experience does not mean delaying every action. Inquiry, change and checking can move together.

options.text: Drop the inquiry and send a reminder, since any action is better than none.
options.feedback: A reminder may help some people, but repeating the same message can repeat the same barrier. Start by understanding the experience.

decisions.scenario: You are reviewing a form used by people from many communities. A teammate proposes offering extra help only to people whose names look unfamiliar.
decisions.question: What is your next step?

options.text: Agree, since it targets help where it is probably needed.
options.feedback: The lesson says not to assume needs from a name, appearance, disability, language or community. That guess can be wrong in both directions.

options.text: Suggest asking everyone respectfully about needs and preferences, offering choices within the process, and confirming the response works.
options.feedback: Yes. Ask, offer choices, confirm. That respects the person and avoids guessing from surface features.

options.text: Give everyone the identical format so the form treats everyone the same.
options.feedback: The same format does not mean everyone can use it. Equity asks what people need in order to participate meaningfully.

ordering.scenario: You have chosen your work example and want to use the approach from part 1.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Make a reasonable inquiry into how people experience it
Choose one ordinary work example you can examine safely
Try an appropriate change and check what happened
Write its purpose and what the person needs to be able to do
ordering.feedback: Start with an example, describe the purpose and the person's task, then inquire, try a change and check what happened. The lesson warns against both guessing and waiting for perfect information.

points: You do not need to know every culture or run a whole program to begin; you need to notice, ask and follow through.
The National CLAS Standards are a framework for organizations; this curriculum connects them to your own work.
Learning is voluntary and private: keep names, health information and other private details out of your notes.

keyPoints.chapter: Choose something you can work with
points: Pick one ordinary part of your work, or use the sample service-planning notice.
Write the organization's purpose and, separately, what the person needs to be able to do.
An observation such as 'some people do not respond' raises questions; it does not explain why.
Standard 1 asks for services people can understand, that respect them and that respond to their communication needs.
The focus is the person's experience, not only whether information was sent.
Do not assume needs from a name, appearance, disability or language: ask, offer choices and confirm.
Standard 1 is the purpose; 2 to 4 cover leadership and workforce; 5 to 8 communication; 9 to 15 engagement, improvement and accountability.
A dependable offer of assistance needs a process, trained staff, resources and monitoring behind it.
Good practice includes telling a change within your authority from one that needs coordination or approval.
Sending the same notice more often can repeat the same barrier.
Begin by understanding how people experience the notice, without assuming why anyone did not respond.
Inquiry does not mean waiting for perfect information: inquire reasonably, try a change, check what happened.
Note your work example, who needs to use it, and what successful participation looks like from their side.
Keep the note general and free of personal information.
Next: the difference between an observation and an assumption.

jobAid.title: Start with the person and the purpose
jobAid.useWhen: Use when you pick up any notice, form, instruction or process and want to check it from the person's side.

sections.heading: Before
items: Choose one ordinary, non-sensitive work example, or use the sample notice.
Write one sentence: what is the organization trying to do?
Write a second sentence: what does the person need to understand and do?

sections.heading: During
items: Check the experience, not just delivery: an accurate letter can still be hard to use.
Do not assume needs from a name, appearance, disability, language or community.
Ask respectfully, offer choices within the available process, and confirm the response works.

sections.heading: After
items: Note the example, the people who need to use it, and what successful participation looks like.
Make a reasonable inquiry, try an appropriate change, check what happened.
Decide whether the change is within your authority or needs coordination.

remember: Giving everyone the same format does not tell you whether everyone can use it.
A response pattern is a question to explore, not an explanation.
askWho: Your supervisor, for what you can change within your role.
The responsible program area, for how a notice or process was tested.

modules.outcome: After this part you can separate what you observed from what you assumed, and write a respectful question that leaves room for the person's explanation.

recall.question: Part 2 asked you to write three things about your work example. Which set is right?

options.text: One observation, one assumption to set aside, and one respectful question.
options.feedback: Yes. Then identify an appropriate way to get the answer within your role, without guessing.

options.text: The person's culture, their likely preference, and the rule that follows from it.
options.feedback: The lesson warned against turning general information about a community into a rule about an individual. Ask instead.

options.text: The deadline, the penalty and the reminder schedule.
options.feedback: Requirements still matter, but the task was to notice barriers and ask without assumptions, not to tighten enforcement.

recall.question: Someone has not returned a form. Which opening did part 2 recommend?

options.text: Ask why they failed to return the form.
options.feedback: That asks the person to defend their behavior. The lesson preferred an opening that gives information and leaves room for an explanation.

options.text: Explain the form's purpose, ask whether they received it, and offer help finding a usable way to respond.
options.feedback: Right. It provides information, checks delivery and offers support, while keeping any requirement clear.

options.text: Assume the form was too hard and send an easier version.
options.feedback: That is still an interpretation. Until you ask, you do not know whether delivery, timing, format or something else was the barrier.

decisions.scenario: In a team meeting a colleague says, 'People who do not reply are just not interested.' The only fact is that no reply was received.
decisions.question: What do you say next?

options.text: Agree, because a missing reply speaks for itself.
options.feedback: A missing reply is an observation. 'Not interested' assigns a motive without evidence. Keep the two apart.

options.text: Ask what is known about delivery, understanding, timing and the response methods available.
options.feedback: Yes. That describes what is known and turns the gap into questions you can look into through the right route.

options.text: Suggest that people from that community probably prefer another process.
options.feedback: That swaps one assumption for another. General community knowledge is not a rule about an individual; ask the person.

decisions.scenario: You are about to contact a person who has not responded, and your role permits the contact.
decisions.question: How do you open?

options.text: 'Why have you failed to return the form? The deadline has passed.'
options.feedback: This asks the person to defend themselves before they have any information. It invites silence, not an explanation.

options.text: Explain the form's purpose, ask whether they received it, and offer help finding a response method they can use.
options.feedback: Right. You give information first and create room for their perspective, while the requirement stays clear.

options.text: Tell them the deadline has been extended so there is no pressure.
options.feedback: Do not promise an extension or exception you cannot authorize. Explain what you can do next and who will review it.

options.text: Ask them to describe their personal circumstances so you can understand.
options.feedback: Ask only for what the task needs. The lesson says not to require private information that is not needed.

decisions.scenario: You work on policy and data and have no direct contact with people who receive services. A new process is about to launch.
decisions.question: How does inquiry apply to you?

options.text: It does not; inquiry is for front-line staff.
options.feedback: The lesson says inquiry matters in policy, data, contracts and communications too. Ask how the process was tested and whose experience informed it.

options.text: Ask how the process was tested, whose experience informed it, which access needs were considered and where feedback is recorded.
options.feedback: Yes. Those questions fit your role and point you to the appropriate people rather than guessing.

options.text: Reach out directly to a few people who receive services to hear what they think.
options.feedback: Consult the appropriate people rather than contacting someone outside your responsibilities. Use the approved engagement routes.

decisions.scenario: A family arrives for a meeting. A teammate quietly suggests speaking mainly to the older relative, since 'that is how that community does things'.
decisions.question: What do you do?

options.text: Follow the suggestion to be culturally respectful.
options.feedback: Culture can shape expectations, but it does not determine any one person's preferences. Deciding for them is still an assumption.

options.text: Ask the person whom they would like involved and how they want to participate.
options.feedback: Right. Curiosity about the individual replaces a community generalization, and the person keeps their say.

options.text: Speak only to the person and keep the relative out of it entirely.
options.feedback: The lesson does not say to exclude anyone. It says to ask whom the person wants involved rather than deciding for them.

ordering.scenario: You have noticed something that is not working in your work example.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Write a respectful question that invites the person's perspective
Describe what you observed, without assigning a motive
Identify an appropriate way to get the answer within your role
Name the assumption you need to set aside
ordering.feedback: Observation first, then the assumption you are setting aside, then a respectful question, then the appropriate route to the answer. If you have no direct access, name the gap and find who can help.

points: Start with an observation you could state without assigning a motive.
'They do not care' and 'they cannot understand it' are both interpretations until you know more.
A respectful inquiry begins by acknowledging what you do not know.
Responding takes steps: receive the notice, recognize its purpose, understand the options, decide, respond.
A difficulty at any one step can look like a lack of interest from the other end.
Look for strengths too: a working communication method, a trusted support, a community organization with relationships.

keyPoints.chapter: Culture is a starting point for curiosity
points: Culture can shape communication and expectations; it does not determine any one person's preferences.
Ask whom the person wants involved; offer time and a way to ask questions instead of reading silence as agreement.
Familiar procedures feel simple to the people who use them daily and may be new to everyone else.
'Why have you failed to return the form?' asks the person to defend themselves.
Explain the purpose, ask whether they received it, and offer help finding a usable way to respond.
Keep requirements clear, and do not promise an extension or exception you cannot authorize.

keyPoints.chapter: Apply inquiry to your own role
points: In policy, data, contracts or communications, ask how the process was tested and whose experience informed it.
Consult the appropriate people rather than guessing or contacting someone outside your responsibilities.
Supervisors can make it safe to ask; managers can look for repeated barriers; directors can check resources and accountability.
Write one observation, one assumption to set aside and one respectful question.
If you cannot reach the people affected, name the gap and identify who can help.
Next: following a language-assistance request through an encounter.

jobAid.title: Notice barriers and ask without assumptions
jobAid.useWhen: Use when a response is missing, an appointment is missed, or you are tempted to explain someone's behavior.

sections.heading: Before
items: Write down what you actually observed. Leave out motives.
Name the assumption you are tempted to make, and set it aside.
List the steps the person had to complete: receive, recognize the purpose, understand the options, decide, respond.

sections.heading: During
items: Explain the purpose first. Ask whether the information was received.
Offer help finding a response method they can use.
Ask whom the person wants involved and how they want to participate.
Keep requirements clear; do not promise exceptions you cannot authorize.

sections.heading: After
items: Record only what the task needs; no unnecessary private information.
If you have no direct access to the people affected, name the gap and find who can help.
Raise repeated barriers through the appropriate route.

remember: An observation describes; an assumption explains. Keep them apart.
Community knowledge is a starting point for curiosity, not a rule about an individual.
askWho: Your supervisor, when you are uncertain and want to talk it through.
The responsible program area, for how a process was tested and where feedback is recorded.
Approved engagement or accessibility review processes, for perspectives you cannot reach directly.

modules.outcome: After this part you can trace a language-assistance request from the offer through the request, the arrangement, the conversation and the follow-up, and spot where it could fail.

recall.question: An assistance request was sent, but nobody has confirmed the arrangement. What did part 3 say should happen?

options.text: Assume it is handled; the usual address always responds.
options.feedback: A sent request is not a confirmed arrangement. Someone needs to own the follow-through and a backup if it fails.

options.text: Check it through the approved process, tell the person what will happen, and escalate if needed.
options.feedback: Right. Confirm, communicate, escalate: that keeps the person informed without promising something outside your authority.

options.text: Plan to ask a family member to interpret if nobody arrives.
options.feedback: A chosen support person and a qualified interpreter have different roles. Follow the applicable requirements rather than improvising.

recall.question: What did part 3 say about checking whether the person understood the next step?

options.text: Repeat the same wording more loudly until they confirm.
options.feedback: If the explanation was unclear, try a different way. Repeating the same words louder does not add clarity.

options.text: Say you want to check your own explanation was clear, then invite them to say what they understand will happen.
options.feedback: Yes. Framing it as checking your explanation avoids making the person feel tested or blamed.

options.text: Skip it, since asking could feel like a test.
options.feedback: Checking understanding matters. The lesson's point is to do it in a way that does not feel like testing or blaming.

decisions.scenario: You are reviewing the sample notice before it goes out. It lists a date and a phone number but says nothing about communication assistance.
decisions.question: What do you check first?

options.text: Whether the phone number is correct.
options.feedback: Accuracy matters, but the lesson's review asks whether assistance is visible, whether the request method is usable, and who responds.

options.text: Whether the notice makes assistance visible, whether the request method is usable, and whether someone is responsible for responding.
options.feedback: Right. Standards 5, 6 and 7 work together: an available service does little good if nobody knows about it or can request it.

options.text: Whether the notice is short enough to fit on one page.
options.feedback: Length is not the issue here. A short notice that hides the assistance offer still leaves the barrier in place.

decisions.scenario: A person arrives for a planning conversation with a relative who says they have been helping with communication. No interpreter has been arranged.
decisions.question: What is your next step?

options.text: Let the relative interpret, since the person seems comfortable with them.
options.feedback: The CLAS framework discourages using untrained individuals as interpreters. A chosen support and an interpreter are different roles.

options.text: Explain the available assistance, ask about the person's preferences, and follow the approved process for appropriate assistance.
options.feedback: Yes. Treat both people respectfully, keep the person involved in decisions, and use the applicable arrangements and contingency process.

options.text: Ask the relative to step out so the conversation can be done properly.
options.feedback: The lesson does not say to exclude a chosen support person. Clarify roles; do not remove the support the person wants.

options.text: Use a translation app on your phone to get through today's conversation.
options.feedback: Do not improvise with an unapproved automated tool for a consequential conversation. Follow the approved contingency and escalation route.

decisions.scenario: An interpreter is present. The conversation is moving quickly and the person has gone quiet.
decisions.question: What do you do?

options.text: Ask the interpreter to find out whether the person is following.
options.feedback: Address the person directly, not the interpreter. Avoid speaking about the person as though they are not present.

options.text: Slow down, give information in manageable portions, allow time for interpretation, and check whether the method is working.
options.feedback: Right. Clear language, smaller portions, time for questions and a check on the communication method itself.

options.text: Finish quickly to respect everyone's time, then send a written summary.
options.feedback: A written summary does not fix a conversation that did not work. Check now whether communication is working, and respond if it is not.

decisions.scenario: For the third time this month, an assistance arrangement for your team fell through at the last minute.
decisions.question: Beyond handling today's situation, what do you do?

options.text: Keep a private workaround ready so it does not catch you out again.
options.feedback: Staff should not have to solve the same preventable problem repeatedly. A private workaround hides the pattern from the people who could fix it.

options.text: Raise the pattern through the appropriate channel, without personal details.
options.feedback: Yes. Recurring difficulty is organizational information. Raising it connects to leadership, resources and improvement.

options.text: Stop offering assistance until the process becomes reliable.
options.feedback: Withholding the offer removes the person's access. Keep following the approved process and raise the pattern.

ordering.scenario: You are tracing an assistance request through the whole encounter.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: During the conversation, address the person directly and check understanding
Afterwards, confirm the next step in a form the person can use
Make the assistance offer visible and the request method usable
Arrange assistance early and confirm it, with a plan if it fails
ordering.feedback: Before: make the offer visible, then arrange and confirm. During: speak to the person and check understanding. After: confirm the next step in a usable form, and raise any repeated difficulty.

points: Standard 5: timely assistance at no cost; Standard 6: tell people about it orally and in writing; Standard 7: competent assistance.
Assistance is useful only when someone can find it, request it and receive it in time to participate.
This lesson sets no new vendor, reimbursement or approval rule; use current agency procedures.
Check that the notice makes assistance visible, that the request method is usable, and that someone responds.
Ask about preferred language and communication needs through an approved process; do not assume from a name, accent or brief conversation.
A request is not complete when sent: confirm the arrangement and know what to do if it fails.
Treat the person and their chosen support respectfully; do not assume a family member is qualified to interpret.
The framework discourages using untrained individuals and minors as interpreters; follow applicable laws and procedures.
An interpreter conveys communication accurately; a support person provides the support the person wants. Clarify the roles.
Address the person directly, use clear language in manageable portions, and allow time for interpretation and questions.
Check understanding by checking your own explanation, then try a different way if it was unclear.
If assistance is unavailable or unsuitable, use the approved contingency and escalation process; do not improvise.
Confirm the next step in a form the person can use.
Record operational information only in approved systems; a learning worksheet is not a record.
Raise delays or repeated difficulty through the appropriate channel.
A sent request that nobody confirmed leaves the barrier unresolved.
For your example, map where assistance is offered, how it is requested, who responds and how completion is confirmed.
Next: whether people can find, access, understand, use and act on the information itself.

jobAid.title: Make language assistance usable
jobAid.useWhen: Use before, during and after any conversation where language or communication assistance may be needed.

sections.heading: Before
items: Does the notice or invitation make assistance visible and say how to request it?
Ask about preferred language and communication needs through the approved process. Do not assume from a name, accent or short chat.
Arrange assistance early; confirm the language, setting, timing and what the assignment needs.
A sent request is not a confirmed one. Know who confirms and what happens if it fails.

sections.heading: During
items: Speak to the person, not about them.
Use clear language in small portions; allow time for interpretation and questions.
Check your own explanation: 'I want to make sure I explained the next step clearly. What do you understand will happen?'
If assistance is missing or unsuitable, use the approved contingency route. No children, bystanders or unapproved tools.

sections.heading: After
items: Confirm the next step in a form the person can use.
Record only in approved systems, with privacy protections.
Raise delays or repeated problems through the appropriate channel.

remember: A chosen support person and a qualified interpreter have different roles.
Everyday conversation and a complex service decision are different tasks.
askWho: The responsible program area, for the current assistance procedure and contingency route.
Your supervisor, when an arrangement is still unconfirmed close to the conversation.

modules.outcome: After this part you can review a notice or instruction with five questions (find, access, understand, use, act) and propose one change, one specialist review and one usability check.

recall.question: Part 4 gave five review questions for a piece of information. Which list is right?

options.text: Can the person find it, access it, understand it, use it and act on it?
options.feedback: Yes. They are a practical review aid, not a replacement for technical accessibility testing or translation review.

options.text: Print it, post it, mail it, email it, text it.
options.feedback: Channels matter, but the five questions are about the person's experience of the information, not how it is distributed.

options.text: Shorten it, simplify it, translate it, approve it, send it.
options.feedback: Some of those may be steps you take, but the lesson's five questions are about what the person can do with the information.

recall.question: A colleague wants to publish the notice as an image so the layout stays consistent. What did part 4 say?

options.text: Fine, as long as the wording is unchanged.
options.feedback: An image of text can be unreadable to assistive technology, and it does nothing about unclear wording.

options.text: Use an accessible format and the appropriate checks; an image of text may exclude people.
options.feedback: Right. Check the document people will actually receive, including any exported version.

options.text: Only a problem if someone complains.
options.feedback: Standard 8 asks for understandable materials up front. Use the established review process rather than waiting for a complaint.

decisions.scenario: You are revising the sample notice. The opening sentence is full of acronyms and internal references.
decisions.question: What do you change first?

options.text: Delete the technical terms and the required details so the notice is shorter.
options.feedback: Shorter is not necessarily clearer or complete. Keep essential rights, choices and requirements; explain terms when they first appear.

options.text: Start with the purpose and the next step, explain necessary terms, and keep the required meaning intact.
options.feedback: Yes. Purpose first, then the action, the date and how to ask questions or request assistance, with required content preserved.

options.text: Keep the wording and add a glossary page at the end.
options.feedback: A glossary leaves the reader to decode the opening before they know why they are reading. Explain terms where they appear and lead with purpose.

decisions.scenario: The notice needs to reach people who read languages other than English. A teammate suggests pasting it into a free online translator.
decisions.question: What do you say?

options.text: Good idea; it is fast and free.
options.feedback: Do not send confidential information into an unapproved translation service. Use the qualified review and the approved process.

options.text: Simplify the English source first, then use the approved qualified translation process.
options.feedback: Right. A translated document can still be hard to understand if the source is complicated, and the translation route must be approved.

options.text: Skip translation; a plain-English version is enough for everyone.
options.feedback: An easy-to-read English version does not meet every language need. Plain language and translation solve related but different problems.

decisions.scenario: You have improved a draft of an official, regulated form. Your version is clearer.
decisions.question: What is your next step?

options.text: Replace the current form with your version so people benefit right away.
options.feedback: A regulated notice or official form may require review before use. Check whether the change is within your authority.

options.text: Preserve the required content and route the revision to the person responsible for review.
options.feedback: Yes. You improved the draft; approval belongs to the responsible role. That keeps the required meaning safe.

options.text: Drop the idea, since you cannot approve it yourself.
options.feedback: Not being the approver does not make the improvement worthless. Send a proposal with the required content preserved.

decisions.scenario: A new instruction says: 'Contact the department before the deadline.' It does not say how, or what must be done by that date.
decisions.question: What do you check?

options.text: Whether the deadline is correct.
options.feedback: Correctness matters, but the person still cannot act. The lesson asks whether they can use the information to complete a step.

options.text: Whether the person can act: a named contact route, the action that is due, and how to ask for help or assistance.
options.feedback: Right. Make the next step concrete with the approved contact details, and keep a way to request assistance.

options.text: Whether it fits the house style.
options.feedback: Style is secondary. The question is whether a person can act: how to contact, what to do, and by when.

ordering.scenario: You are reviewing a notice with the questions from part 4.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would check them.
steps: Can the person understand it?
Can the person use it and act on it?
Can the person find it?
Can the person access it in a format they can use?
ordering.feedback: Find, access, understand, then use and act. Each question only matters if the one before it is answered: nobody can act on information they cannot find or open.

points: Standard 8 covers understandable print and digital materials and signage in the languages people use.
Five questions: can the person find it, access it, understand it, use it and act on it?
The questions are a review aid, not a substitute for accessibility testing or translation review.
An assistance statement that lives on a website but not on the notice is hard to find when it is needed.
Images of text, uncaptioned video, mouse-only forms and digital-only instructions can all exclude people.
Use the established review process and check the document people will actually receive, including exports.
Lead with purpose and action; explain necessary terms when they first appear.
Plain language is not permission to remove rights, choices or requirements.
Simplify the source before translating, use the approved qualified process, and never paste confidential text into an unapproved tool.
Make the next step concrete: how to confirm, how to request assistance, where to ask questions.
Use approved contact details; this lesson invents no new contact or process.
A regulated notice or official form may need review before use; route your revision to the responsible role.
Compare revisions for clarity, accessibility, required meaning and a way to request assistance.
Identify one change you can propose, one item for specialist review and one way to check usability.
Feedback from people who use the information should be accessible, voluntary and clear about how it will be used.
Note the barrier, the proposed change, the necessary review and the expected benefit.
One automated check or one positive comment does not make a document fully accessible.
Next: the roles, resources and decisions that make the improvement sustainable.

jobAid.title: Make information accessible and actionable
jobAid.useWhen: Use when you draft, review or approve a notice, form, instruction, web page or sign.

sections.heading: Find
items: Is the assistance offer on the notice itself, not only somewhere on a website?
Do links and headings say what they are for?

sections.heading: Access
items: Is it real text, not an image of text?
Captions and a transcript for video; keyboard access for forms; a non-digital route where needed.
Check the exported version people will actually receive.

sections.heading: Understand
items: Purpose and next step first. Explain terms when they first appear.
Keep rights, choices and requirements intact.
Simplify the English source before translation; use the approved qualified translation process.

sections.heading: Use and act
items: Name a usable contact route and the action due by the date.
Include how to request communication assistance, using approved wording and contact details.
Check whether the change is within your authority; route regulated content to the responsible reviewer.

remember: Shorter is not automatically clearer or complete.
One automated check does not make a document accessible.
askWho: The appropriate accessibility support, for technical review.
The approved translation route, for other languages.
The person responsible for the official notice, for review and approval.

modules.outcome: After this part you can sort an improvement into what you can change yourself, what needs coordination or review, and what needs someone else's decision, and name the responsible role for each.

recall.question: You find a barrier in an official notice but cannot change the requirement. What did part 5 recommend?

options.text: Change it anyway, because the goal is important.
options.feedback: An important goal does not expand your authority. Preserve the requirement and send a supported proposal.

options.text: Describe the barrier, propose a revision that keeps the required meaning, and identify the responsible role.
options.feedback: Yes. That moves the work forward without exceeding authority or abandoning the concern.

options.text: Leave it, because you cannot approve the change.
options.feedback: You can still document the barrier and recommend a next step. A well-described problem is a real contribution.

recall.question: Part 5 asked you to sort proposed actions into three categories. Which are they?

options.text: What you can change, what needs coordination or review, and what needs a decision by someone with different authority.
options.feedback: Right. For each one, name the responsible role, the resource needed and a reasonable next step.

options.text: Urgent, important and optional.
options.feedback: Priority is useful, but the lesson's categories are about authority: yours, shared, or someone else's.

options.text: Front line, supervisor and director.
options.feedback: Those are perspectives the lesson explored, not the three categories for sorting an action.

decisions.scenario: You prepare information for a program. The same unclear instruction has caused confusion in several encounters this month.
decisions.question: What do you do with that?

options.text: Handle each confused person as they come; it is part of the job.
options.feedback: Avoid carrying an unresolved access problem privately from one encounter to the next. A pattern is something others can act on.

options.text: Describe the pattern with clear evidence, protecting personal information, and raise it through the appropriate route.
options.feedback: Yes. Observation, a clear description and a supported suggestion give the responsible role something concrete to act on.

options.text: Rewrite the instruction and start using your version.
options.feedback: You may be able to propose a revision, but an approved instruction may need review. Preserve the required meaning and route it.

decisions.scenario: You supervise a team. A staff member says a person 'just does not engage' and asks what to do.
decisions.question: How do you coach?

options.text: Suggest moving on if the person does not engage soon.
options.feedback: That accepts a label instead of looking for the access barrier. Help staff tell an assumption about motivation from a barrier.

options.text: Ask what they observed, what they asked, what remains uncertain and what support they need.
options.feedback: Right. Coaching through questions makes room for uncertainty and turns a label back into something to investigate.

options.text: Give them the answer so they do not have to work it out.
options.feedback: Standard 4 is about learning connected to real decisions. Questions help staff practice, not just receive a definition.

decisions.scenario: You manage a process. An instruction tells staff to offer language assistance, but the one person who arranges it is often unavailable.
decisions.question: What do you look at?

options.text: Remind staff to keep offering assistance regardless.
options.feedback: An instruction to offer assistance is incomplete if staff have no workable way to arrange it. Fix the process, not just the reminder.

options.text: Clarify who owns the arrangement, how requests are tracked, what happens when the usual contact is away, and whether capacity is enough.
options.feedback: Yes. Ownership, tracking, continuity and capacity make the process dependable, not just stated.

options.text: Compare participation across groups and assign the cause.
options.feedback: A difference in participation is a reason to investigate, not proof of one cause. Part 7 covers reading evidence carefully.

decisions.scenario: You advise leadership. A proposal suggests relying on a bilingual employee to interpret informally because of their background.
decisions.question: What goes in your advice?

options.text: Support it; it saves money and the employee speaks the language.
options.feedback: Identity is not qualification. The lesson warns against assuming one employee represents a community or should interpret informally.

options.text: Frame the access problem, the evidence and uncertainty, the options, and what each option requires, including proper roles and support.
options.feedback: Right. Clear framing lets leadership decide with capability, preparation and appropriate role assignments in view.

options.text: Recommend that leadership simply issue a policy that assistance must be offered.
options.feedback: A policy statement without resources, trained staff and a workable process does not make assistance dependable. Say what each option requires.

ordering.scenario: You have spotted unclear wording in an official notice you cannot approve.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Identify the responsible role
Describe the barrier you observed
Send the proposal for review and ask about the next step
Draft a revision that preserves the required meaning
ordering.feedback: Describe the barrier, draft a revision that keeps the required meaning, identify the responsible role, then send it for review. Clarify ownership and resources rather than assuming approval.

points: Some improvements are in your control; others depend on authority, resources or coordination.
Standards 2 to 4 cover governance, leadership and workforce; Standard 9 ties goals, policies and accountability to operations.
The examples describe possible contributions, not new duties; use your actual role and current procedures.

keyPoints.chapter: If your contribution is an everyday task
points: Begin with careful observation, a respectful question, a well-supported suggestion and follow-through on what you own.
Describe the barrier, preserve the required meaning, and send the proposed improvement to the person responsible.
Do not carry an unresolved access problem privately from one encounter to the next; raise the pattern.
Coach with questions: what did you observe, what did you ask, what is uncertain, what support do you need?
Help staff tell an access barrier from an assumption about motivation.
Useful learning connects to real decisions, such as reviewing a notice or an assistance request.

keyPoints.chapter: If you manage a process or resources
points: Clarify who maintains the text, who arranges assistance, how requests are tracked and how problems are reviewed.
Ask whether the process still works when the usual contact is unavailable; consider workload and capacity.
A difference in participation is a reason to investigate, not proof of one cause.

keyPoints.chapter: If you set direction or advise leadership
points: Make expectations visible in policy, planning, resources and accountability.
Do not assume one employee represents a community or should interpret informally because of their identity.
Frame a decision: the access problem, the evidence and uncertainty, the options, and what each requires.
Sort actions: within your responsibilities, needing coordination or review, or needing someone else's decision.
Name the responsible role, the resource or information needed and a reasonable next step.
Neither changing a requirement on your own nor leaving the problem unraised is a complete response.
A role map makes the improvement realistic and shows who has not yet been heard.
Next: how the people affected can inform a change before the decision is made.

cardDescriptions.description: Part 5 card titled 'Individual action needs support', showing on the left a photo of three colleagues at a table reviewing a printed diagram beside a laptop and a notebook, one pointing at the page, and on the right three numbered points: Individual action needs organizational support; 2–4: leadership and workforce; 9: goals and accountability.

cardDescriptions.chapter: If your contribution is an everyday task
cardDescriptions.description: Part 5 card titled 'If your contribution is an everyday task' with no photo, three numbered points across the card (Notice and describe; Propose a supported improvement; Stay within your authority) and the reminder 'Pause whenever you want to think, practice or make a note.'

Part 5 card titled 'If you supervise people', showing on the left a photo of two people in conversation in a sunlit office, one seated in an armchair listening while the other, who uses a wheelchair, speaks and gestures, and on the right three numbered points: Coach through questions; Make room for uncertainty; Connect learning to real decisions.

cardDescriptions.description: Part 5 card titled 'If you manage a process or resources', showing on the left a photo of three colleagues at a table reviewing a printed diagram beside a laptop and a notebook, one pointing at the page, and on the right three numbered points: Clarify ownership and resources; Check capacity and continuity; Review recurring patterns.

cardDescriptions.chapter: If you set direction or advise leadership
cardDescriptions.description: Part 5 card titled 'If you set direction or advise leadership' with no photo, three numbered points across the card (Make expectations visible; Equip and support the workforce; Do not assign roles by identity) and the reminder 'Pause whenever you want to think, practice or make a note.'

jobAid.title: Connect your role with organizational responsibility
jobAid.useWhen: Use when you have found a barrier and need to decide what you can do about it and who else must be involved.

sections.heading: Sort the action
items: Within my responsibilities: I can change this now.
Needs coordination or review: who must look at it first?
Needs a decision by someone with different authority: who?

sections.heading: For each action
items: Name the responsible role, not a person's name.
Note the resource or information needed.
Write one reasonable next step. If ownership is unclear, clarifying it is the next step.

sections.heading: By perspective
items: Everyday task: observe, ask, propose with evidence, follow through on what you own.
Supervisor: coach with questions; make room for uncertainty and escalation.
Manager: clarify ownership, tracking, continuity and capacity.
Leadership adviser: frame the problem, the evidence, the options and what each requires.

remember: An important goal does not expand your authority; silence does not discharge your responsibility.
Identity is not a qualification; do not assign interpreting or representation by background.
askWho: Your supervisor, for what you can decide in your role.
The owner of the notice or process, for review and approval.
The responsible office, when ownership is unclear.

modules.outcome: After this part you can plan accessible input on a decision while it is still open, say honestly what can and cannot change, and explain how people will hear what happened.

recall.question: A team wants input on a revised notice. Which timing did part 6 recommend?

options.text: After approval and distribution, so people react to the real thing.
options.feedback: By then participation arrives too late to influence the decision. Later evaluation helps, but it serves a different purpose.

options.text: Before approval, with a clear statement of what can change and a plan to report back.
options.feedback: Yes. Input matters when there is a real opportunity to act on it, and closing the loop keeps trust.

options.text: Only if someone complains about the first version.
options.feedback: Standards 12 and 13 ask for partnership in design, not just complaint handling. Invite input while the decision is open.

recall.question: What did part 6 say about asking one community member to speak for everyone?

options.text: It is efficient and usually accurate.
options.feedback: One perspective can be valuable without representing every experience. Ask whose perspectives are missing.

options.text: One person cannot be assumed to speak for every person with a disability, every language community or every family.
options.feedback: Right. Look for the experiences that are missing, especially people who had trouble with the original information.

options.text: It is fine as long as the person is a professional.
options.feedback: Do not automatically substitute the views of professionals or family members for the person's own perspective.

decisions.scenario: Your team is revising the notice. A required time limit cannot change, but the wording, layout and assistance explanation can.
decisions.question: How do you invite input?

options.text: Ask what people would change about the notice, without mentioning the fixed time limit.
options.feedback: Asking people to choose something that is not open can damage trust. Say honestly what can change and what must stay.

options.text: Say what is open to change, what is fixed, how input will be considered, who decides and when people will hear back.
options.feedback: Yes. A constrained decision can still benefit from meaningful participation when the boundaries are honest.

options.text: Skip input, since the most important part cannot change anyway.
options.feedback: Wording, layout and the assistance explanation are open. That is real room for people to improve the decision.

decisions.scenario: An online survey about the notice got plenty of responses, all positive. Someone suggests the review is done.
decisions.question: What do you check?

options.text: Nothing; the numbers are good.
options.feedback: People who readily answer an online survey may not represent those who had difficulty accessing the original information.

options.text: Whose experience is missing, and whether there is an accessible way to hear from them through the approved process.
options.feedback: Right. Ask whose perspectives are absent and offer appropriate ways to participate, including routes that are not online.

options.text: Whether the survey could be sent out a second time to get more replies.
options.feedback: More of the same replies does not fill the gap. The question is who is missing, not how many answered.

decisions.scenario: You are setting up a feedback session. Someone proposes telling people that services depend on taking part, to boost attendance.
decisions.question: What do you say?

options.text: Agree; participation is important enough.
options.feedback: Respect a person's choice not to participate, and never make access to services appear dependent on giving feedback.

options.text: Keep it voluntary; explain what is asked, how it will be used and any limits on confidentiality; follow the rules on reimbursement.
options.feedback: Yes. Usable, voluntary participation with clear explanations, following privacy, records and payment rules.

options.text: Offer a cash payment to anyone who attends.
options.feedback: If compensation is available, use the established rules. Do not promise a payment you cannot authorize.

decisions.scenario: The team adds an online response form and plans to remove the telephone option to keep things simple. Earlier feedback praised the phone route.
decisions.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: Remove the phone option; the online form is more modern.
options.feedback: A redesign can remove a feature some people depend on. Improving one route does not justify removing another.

options.text: Keep the phone option alongside the new form, and report back on what changed and why.
options.feedback: Right. Listen for assets as well as problems, preserve what works, and close the loop with the people who gave input.

options.text: Ask people to vote on which single route to keep.
options.feedback: Forcing one channel assumes it will work for everyone. Different preferences can coexist; look for choices that support participation.

ordering.scenario: You are planning input on a decision that is still open.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Offer accessible, voluntary ways to take part through the approved process
Explain what changed, what did not, and why
Describe the decision: what can change, what is fixed, who decides
Ask whose experience is missing
ordering.feedback: Describe the decision honestly, work out who is missing, make participation usable, then close the loop. Partnership continues into implementation and evaluation.

keyPoints.chapter: Ask before the decision is settled
points: Feedback requested after approval and distribution arrives too late to influence the decision.
Standard 12: understand community assets and needs; Standard 13: partner in design, implementation and evaluation.
You do not need to organize a group yourself; identify the established route and the people responsible.
Before asking, describe what is open, what must remain, how input will be considered, who decides and when people hear back.
Asking people to choose something that is not open can damage trust.
Ask whose experience is missing; one person cannot speak for every community or family.
Consider format, language, communication support, timing, location, technology and effort.
Keep participation voluntary; never make services appear to depend on giving feedback.
Explain what is asked and how it is used; follow privacy, records and reimbursement rules.

keyPoints.chapter: Listen for assets as well as problems
points: Ask what already works, which approaches are trusted and what people want preserved.
Improving one route does not justify removing another.
When feedback differs, describe the difference instead of forcing agreement.
Explain what changed, what did not and why, without exposing personal information.
Acknowledge suggestions that cannot be adopted and name the constraint or next step.
Partnership continues into implementation and evaluation; it is not an endorsement of a finished product.
Write the decision needing input, the missing perspectives, an accessible way to obtain input, the responsible role and how people hear back.
If you lack authority to start engagement, make a precise recommendation to the responsible person.
The aim is a better decision and experience, not a participant count.

cardDescriptions.description: Part 6 card titled 'Ask before the decision is settled', showing on the left a photo of three people seated around a meeting-room table with paper cups, one speaking while the others listen, and on the right three numbered points: Input before the decision is settled; 12: community assets and needs; 13: partnership.

Part 6 card titled 'Clarify what can change' with no photo, three numbered points across the card (What can change?; What constraints remain?; Who decides and who is missing?) and the reminder 'Pause whenever you want to think, practice or make a note.'

Part 6 card titled 'Make participation usable', showing on the left a photo of three people seated around a meeting-room table with paper cups, one speaking while the others listen, and on the right three numbered points: Make participation accessible and voluntary; Explain use and privacy limits; Use approved engagement arrangements.

cardDescriptions.description: Part 6 card titled 'Listen for assets as well as problems', showing on the left a photo of two people talking across an office table, one writing in a notebook while the other speaks, and on the right three numbered points: Preserve what already works; Different preferences can coexist; Avoid assuming one route fits everyone.

Part 6 card titled 'Close the loop' with no photo, three numbered points across the card (Explain what changed and why; Acknowledge ideas not adopted; Continue learning during implementation) and the reminder 'Pause whenever you want to think, practice or make a note.'

jobAid.title: Learn with people affected by the work
jobAid.useWhen: Use before a decision is settled, whenever a change will affect how people receive or use a service.

sections.heading: Before
items: Write the decision. What is open? What is fixed? Who decides? When will people hear back?
List whose experience is missing, including people who had trouble with the original information.
Identify the established engagement route and the role responsible for it.

sections.heading: During
items: Make participation accessible: format, language, communication support, timing, location, technology, effort.
Keep it voluntary. Explain what is asked, how it will be used and any limits on confidentiality.
Make room for the person themselves, including self-advocates and chosen supports.
Ask what works now and what should be preserved.

sections.heading: After
items: Report back: what changed, what did not, and why.
Acknowledge ideas not adopted and name the constraint.
Keep learning during implementation and evaluation.

remember: Honest boundaries make a constrained decision worth consulting on.
Do not promise reimbursement or outcomes you cannot authorize.
askWho: The role responsible for engagement, to arrange accessible participation.
The responsible office, for privacy, records and reimbursement rules.

modules.outcome: After this part you can set a practical aim for an improvement and choose a process question, an experience question and an outcome question to check whether it helped.

recall.question: Part 7 named three kinds of measure. Which set is right?

options.text: Process, experience and outcome.
options.feedback: Yes. Did the action happen, how did people encounter it, and did the intended result improve? Add a balancing question about new burdens.

options.text: Cost, speed and volume.
options.feedback: Those can be tracked, but the lesson's three measures are process, experience and outcome.

options.text: Input, output and feedback.
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but the lesson used process, experience and outcome, each answering a different question.

recall.question: A revised notice got more responses than the old one. What did part 7 say that shows?

options.text: The new wording caused the improvement.
options.feedback: Timing, recipients, contact method and assistance availability may also differ. A difference is a question, not proof of cause.

options.text: A useful observation that needs checking against the denominator, what is missing, and people's experience.
options.feedback: Right. Use the observation while checking its limits before deciding what it means.

options.text: Nothing, because the comparison is not a controlled study.
options.feedback: Imperfect information can still guide inquiry when its limits are clear. Do not dismiss it; examine it.

decisions.scenario: Your team wants to show the revised notice is working. The only number on hand is how many notices were sent.
decisions.question: What do you propose?

options.text: Report the number sent as evidence of improvement.
options.feedback: An action is evidence of implementation, not proof of its effect. Sending a notice does not show anyone could use it.

options.text: Add an experience question and an outcome question alongside the process count, using information that is already available.
options.feedback: Yes. Process, experience and outcome together give a more useful picture than a completion count alone.

options.text: Create a new survey collecting personal details from everyone who received it.
options.feedback: Do not create a new dataset or collect personal information just to complete this learning. Use available, approved information.

decisions.scenario: A colleague says people from one community respond less often, and wants to record each person's likely background from their names to track it.
decisions.question: What do you say?

options.text: Good idea; it will make the pattern visible.
options.feedback: Do not infer language, disability, race or other identity from a name or appearance. Standard 11 is about accurate, reliable data gathered under approved methods.

options.text: Treat the pattern as a prompt to investigate with appropriate input, and use only approved demographic data under applicable privacy rules.
options.feedback: Right. A difference is a reason for inquiry, not a label for a community, and data use must follow approved methods.

options.text: Ignore the pattern until an official study is commissioned.
options.feedback: You do not have to dismiss the observation. Investigate appropriately with the responsible staff and the people affected.

decisions.scenario: A summary table shows results by neighborhood, language and disability. Some cells contain two or three people.
decisions.question: What do you do before sharing it?

options.text: Share it; the more detail the better.
options.feedback: Small groups and combined characteristics can make individuals recognizable. Use the approved protections and reporting rules.

options.text: Apply the approved protections and reporting rules, and explain the limits where information cannot be shared safely.
options.feedback: Yes. When something cannot be shared safely, explain the limitation rather than inventing a conclusion.

options.text: Remove the whole table and report nothing.
options.feedback: Protecting people does not require silence. Use the approved reporting rules and share what can be shared responsibly.

decisions.scenario: You are allowed to try a small change to your own drafting practice, and you want to learn from it.
decisions.question: What goes in the plan?

options.text: Try it, and keep it if nobody complains.
options.feedback: Without a planned review, a temporary fix becomes permanent with nobody checking its effect. Name who reviews and when.

options.text: Identify the barrier, plan the authorized change, try it at a sensible scale, set who reviews the evidence and when, and record the reasoning.
options.feedback: Right. That is the lesson's improvement cycle, with a review step so the next person can see why.

options.text: Roll it out everywhere at once so results come faster.
options.feedback: Scale depends on the work. Try it at an appropriate scale, review what happened, then decide what to keep or adjust.

ordering.scenario: You are planning a manageable improvement.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Try it at an appropriate scale
Identify the barrier
Review what happened and decide what to keep or adjust
Plan an authorized change
ordering.feedback: Identify, plan, try, review. Specify who reviews the evidence and when, and record the reasoning so the next person understands why the change was made.

points: Standards 9, 10 and 11 connect goals, accountability, ongoing assessment and reliable demographic data to improvement.
Start with a specific aim, such as making the next step and assistance options easier to understand.
Fit the aim to your role; do not collect personal information or create a dataset just for this lesson.

keyPoints.chapter: Look at process, experience and outcome
points: Process: did the planned action happen? Experience: how did people encounter it? Outcome: did the intended result improve?
A high response rate does not show that people understood their choices or felt respected.
Ask a balancing question: did the change create a new burden or barrier elsewhere?
More responses to one version does not prove the wording caused it; timing, recipients and assistance may differ.
Ask about the denominator, what is missing, and whether the measure means the same across groups.
Never infer language, disability, race or identity from a name or appearance; data use must follow approved rules.
Small groups and combined characteristics can identify individuals; use approved protections and reporting rules.
When information cannot be shared safely, explain the limitation rather than inventing a conclusion.
Treat a difference as a prompt for inquiry, not a label attached to a community.
Identify the barrier, plan an authorized change, try it at an appropriate scale, review, then keep or adjust.
Name who reviews the evidence and when, so a temporary fix does not quietly become permanent.
Document the reasoning so the next person understands why.
Write a practical aim, one process question, one experience question and one outcome question.
Note the information already available, an important limitation, the responsible role and a review date.
If your role lacks data access, do not work around it; ask whether an approved evaluation exists.

jobAid.title: Use evidence to improve access
jobAid.useWhen: Use when you propose a change and need to say how you will know whether it helped.

sections.heading: Set the aim
items: One specific aim, in plain words.
Fit it to your role and to information that already exists.

sections.heading: Choose the questions
items: Process: did the planned action happen?
Experience: could people understand the next step and get support?
Outcome: did the intended result improve?
Balance: did the change create a new burden elsewhere?

sections.heading: Read the numbers
items: How many people received each version? That is the denominator.
What is missing: undelivered notices, unanswered questions?
Does the measure mean the same thing across groups?
Small counts can swing with a few extra responses.

sections.heading: Protect people
items: Never infer identity from a name or appearance.
Use approved demographic data, methods and privacy rules only.
Protect small groups; explain limits instead of inventing conclusions.

sections.heading: Review
items: Who reviews the evidence, and when?
Record the reasoning for the next person.

remember: An action is evidence of implementation, not proof of effect.
A difference is a question, not a label.
askWho: The responsible team, for what information an evaluation would need.
The responsible office, before any data collection or reporting.

modules.outcome: After this part you can respond to an access concern with acknowledgment, a usable next step and honest limits, and write a progress update that separates actions from results.

recall.question: Someone says they could not understand the notice and could not request assistance. Which response did part 8 recommend?

options.text: Explain that the notice was sent correctly and close the matter.
options.feedback: Sending information does not establish that it was usable. Acknowledge the concern and follow the appropriate process.

options.text: Acknowledge the concern, clarify what they need now, and explain the next step and the responsible route.
options.feedback: Yes. That is usable and honest, without promising outcomes, timing or confidentiality beyond your authority.

options.text: Promise it will be fixed tomorrow and kept completely confidential.
options.feedback: Do not promise an outcome, a deadline you cannot control, or confidentiality beyond what the process permits.

recall.question: A draft update says the new notice 'has solved communication barriers'. What did part 8 say about that?

options.text: Fine, as long as the notice really was revised.
options.feedback: Updating a notice is an action. Evidence that people can use it is a result that still needs checking.

options.text: Separate the action from the result: say what was revised, how usability is being checked and when the next review is.
options.feedback: Right. Honest progress communication explains what was done, what was learned and what happens next.

options.text: Remove the update; progress should stay internal.
options.feedback: Standard 15 asks organizations to communicate progress. The fix is accuracy, not silence.

decisions.scenario: A person tells you they missed a planning conversation because they could not understand the notice. Your first instinct is to check whether it was mailed.
decisions.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Confirm the notice was sent on the right date and tell them so.
options.feedback: Proving delivery does not help the person now and can sound like blame. Acknowledge the concern and ask what they need.

options.text: Acknowledge the concern, ask what they need now, and explain what you can do and who is responsible for the next step.
options.feedback: Yes. Receive the concern respectfully, then follow the applicable process without over-promising.

options.text: Apologize and promise the meeting will be rescheduled this week with full confidentiality.
options.feedback: Do not promise timing or confidentiality beyond your authority and the process's limits. Explain what will happen and who owns it.

decisions.scenario: A concern sounds like it may involve discrimination, but your team's usual route is the general feedback form.
decisions.question: What do you do?

options.text: Log it in the feedback form; that is the process you know.
options.feedback: Do not relabel a concern to fit the process most familiar to you. Get the appropriate guidance and keep the person's channels open.

options.text: Obtain the appropriate guidance on the right route and preserve the person's opportunity to use the available channels.
options.feedback: Right. Discrimination, service failure and accessibility issues may need specific routes. Do not decide for the person which one.

options.text: Tell the person to look up the complaints process online.
options.feedback: Sending someone elsewhere without explaining the route can leave them with no next step. Explain the route clearly and usably.

decisions.scenario: Several people have raised the same unclear instruction this quarter. Each concern was resolved individually.
decisions.question: What else is needed?

options.text: Nothing; every concern was closed.
options.feedback: Resolving each issue may be necessary without addressing the condition that caused it. Recurring concerns should inform improvement.

options.text: Raise the pattern so the instruction itself is reviewed, using approved channels and no personal details.
options.feedback: Yes. Recurring concerns are improvement information. Review the instruction as well as responding to each person.

options.text: Add a note to the form warning people to read carefully.
options.feedback: That shifts the burden to the reader. If several people hit the same barrier, the instruction needs review.

decisions.scenario: You are drafting a progress update about the revised notice. The revision is approved and distributed; usability has not yet been checked.
decisions.question: What do you write?

options.text: 'The new notice has removed communication barriers.'
options.feedback: That claims a result when only the action is confirmed. Keep actions and results separate.

options.text: 'The notice and assistance information were revised after review; usability is being checked and the next review point is set.'
options.feedback: Right. Understandable, honest about limits, and clear about what was done, what was learned and what happens next.

options.text: 'The person who complained has been dealt with and the notice updated.'
options.feedback: Avoid details that could identify someone who raised a concern. Share only what is approved for the audience and purpose.

ordering.scenario: A person raises an access concern with you.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would do them.
steps: Explain what you can do, what happens next and who is responsible
Acknowledge the concern
Follow the applicable process and raise any recurring pattern
Clarify what the person needs now
ordering.feedback: Acknowledge, clarify the immediate need, explain the next step and the responsible route, then follow the process. Urgent safety, legal or service needs use the current urgent procedure.

keyPoints.chapter: Make it possible to raise a concern
points: Standard 14: accessible ways to identify, prevent and resolve complaints; Standard 15: communicate progress.
Know the appropriate route and explain it clearly.
Do not leave someone without a next step just because the issue belongs to another part of the organization.
Acknowledge the concern, clarify what the person needs now, and follow the applicable process.
Do not promise an outcome, a deadline you cannot control, or confidentiality beyond what the process permits.
Do not relabel a concern to fit the process you know; urgent matters use the current urgent procedure.
Can someone find the concern process, understand it and use it in a suitable language and format?
Tell people how receipt is acknowledged, what information is needed and how to ask about progress.
Recurring concerns should inform improvement; review the instruction as well as responding to each person.
Progress communication is understandable, accessible and honest about limits.
Say what was done, what was learned and what happens next.
Updating a notice is an action; evidence that people can use it is a result that needs checking.
Share only what is approved for the audience and purpose; avoid details that could identify someone who raised a concern.
Use the appropriate review process for public communication; this lesson does not authorize publishing for the division.
If a change did not help, explain the next step rather than hiding the result.
A good response acknowledges, gives a usable next step and is honest about responsibility.
Draft a progress statement: the issue, the action, how the effect will be checked, the next review point.
Keep the statement general and suitable for a learning exercise.

keyPoints.chapter: Prepare to bring the work together
points: You now have the elements: the person's task, a barrier to investigate, a response, roles, input, evidence, and a way to respond and report back.
The final part assembles them into one usable plan.
It is not a test of memorizing fifteen numbers; it is practice at a thoughtful decision and a concrete next step.
