jobAid.title: Respond to concerns and share progress
jobAid.useWhen: Use when someone tells you something is not working, and when you write an update about a change.

sections.heading: When a concern is raised
items: Acknowledge it. Do not start by proving the information was sent.
Ask what the person needs now.
Explain what you can do, what happens next and who is responsible.
Do not promise outcomes, deadlines or confidentiality beyond the process.
Urgent safety, legal or service needs: use the current urgent procedure.

sections.heading: Check the route
items: Can people find, understand and use the concern process in a suitable language and format?
Is receipt acknowledged? Is it clear how to ask about progress?
Do not relabel a concern to fit a familiar process; get the right guidance.
Raise recurring concerns so the cause is reviewed.

sections.heading: When you write an update
items: Issue, action taken or proposed, how the effect will be checked, next review point.
Separate the action (notice revised) from the result (people can use it).
Say what is known and what remains uncertain.
No details that could identify a person; use the approved review before publishing.

remember: Sending information does not establish that it was usable.
Clear limits are more useful than broad assurance.
askWho: The responsible office, for the correct concern route and urgent procedures.
The appropriate review process, before any public or organizational statement.

modules.outcome: After this part you can assemble your notes into one improvement plan with an observed barrier, a proposed change, the responsible role, participation, evidence and a follow-up date.

recall.question: Part 9 said to describe the issue in your plan as what?

options.text: An observation, not an assumption about why it happens.
options.feedback: Yes. For the notice: some people have not responded, and the next step and assistance options need review. No conclusion about motives or a single cause.

options.text: A conclusion about the single cause, so the plan is decisive.
options.feedback: The lesson kept uncertainty visible. Naming what you do not know directs the next inquiry; it does not weaken the plan.

options.text: A list of all fifteen standards.
options.feedback: The plan is not a memorization test. Connect the standards that fit the action and consider the wider conditions.

recall.question: Part 9 distinguished completion from effect. Which statement matches?

options.text: Sending a revised document for approval means the barrier is fixed.
options.feedback: Sending it is progress; approval is another step; evidence that people can use it is a further question.

options.text: Sending for approval is progress, approval is another step, and evidence of use is a further question.
options.feedback: Right. Recognizing each stage helps you describe progress accurately.

options.text: Nothing counts until the effect is proven.
options.feedback: Progress can be real at each stage. The point is to describe each stage accurately, not to dismiss it.

decisions.scenario: You are writing the issue statement for your plan. Your notes say some people did not respond to the notice.
decisions.question: How do you write it?

options.text: 'People are not interested in the service-planning conversation.'
options.feedback: That is an assumption. The lesson describes the issue as an observation: some people have not responded, and the next step and assistance options need review.

options.text: 'Some people have not responded; the explanation of the next step and assistance options needs review.'
options.feedback: Yes. An observation plus the thing to examine, without concluding about motives or a single cause.

options.text: 'The wording is the cause, so the wording will be fixed.'
options.feedback: Wording may be part of it, but the lesson warns against treating one cause as proven. Keep uncertainty visible.

decisions.scenario: Your plan proposes adding an online response route to the notice.
decisions.question: What do you check before finalizing?

options.text: That the online form looks modern and loads quickly.
options.feedback: The lesson's check is about barriers: who needs another method, and whether necessary information remains.

options.text: Whether the change creates a new barrier, and that another method remains for people who need one.
options.feedback: Right. Check for unintended barriers: keep an alternative route and keep the necessary information in place.

options.text: Nothing; adding a route can only help.
options.feedback: A new online option can help some people while leaving others without a usable alternative. Check for the new barrier.

decisions.scenario: Your plan is written. The draft notice has not yet been reviewed by the right group, and you are not sure the assistance route is reliably available.
decisions.question: What do you do with those gaps?

options.text: Leave them out so the plan looks complete.
options.feedback: Naming an uncertainty directs the next inquiry. Pretending the issue is resolved does not make it so.

options.text: Record them as uncertainties, with a next inquiry for each and a realistic next step.
options.feedback: Yes. A strong plan can acknowledge uncertainty and still identify a concrete next step.

options.text: Wait to finish the plan until both are resolved.
options.feedback: A manageable, authorized contribution is worthwhile now. Name what you can do and what needs wider coordination.

decisions.scenario: It has been about thirty days and the action in your plan has not started.
decisions.question: What does the follow-up look like?

options.text: Mark the plan complete since the time has passed.
options.feedback: Completion is not the same as effect, and nothing has started. Identify the reason and the next realistic step.

options.text: Note the reason it has not started and the next realistic step, and keep progress and effect separate.
options.feedback: Right. Ask what you tried, what changed, what evidence you have and what remains. If nothing started, say why and what is next.

options.text: Share your full notes, including the people involved, with your team for help.
options.feedback: A follow-up discussion can help, but keep it to a non-sensitive summary with an appropriate colleague or supervisor.

ordering.scenario: You are assembling your improvement plan.
ordering.prompt: Put these in the order you would write them.
steps: Identify the proposed change and the standards it connects to
Describe the issue as an observation
Name the action, the responsible role, the resources and a review point
Describe the intended experience for the person
ordering.feedback: Observation, intended experience, proposed change with its standards, then the workable details: action, owner, resources, review point. Record what remains uncertain and check for new barriers.

keyPoints.chapter: Return to the person and the task
points: Go back to your first notes: has your understanding changed?
The standards give a connected way to think about quality and access; your plan turns that into a manageable contribution.
Use the sample notice if your own example is too sensitive or not ready.
Describe the issue as an observation, not an assumption about motives or a single cause.
Describe the intended experience: understand the purpose, consider choices, request assistance, use a clear response route.
Connect the change to the standards: 1 and 8 for the notice, 5 to 7 for assistance, 2 to 4 and 9 for ownership, 10 to 13 for input and evidence, 14 and 15 for concerns and progress.
Name the action, the role responsible for approval or coordination, the resources needed and a review point.
Record what remains uncertain; it directs the next inquiry.
Check whether the plan creates a new barrier: keep an alternative route, keep necessary information, keep the decision open to input.
Does the plan begin with inquiry, preserve choices, provide a usable assistance route, stay within authority, involve people affected and include a credible check?
A strong answer can acknowledge uncertainty and still name a concrete next step.
The goal is transfer to work, not repeating a definition.
Revisit the plan about thirty days after the action begins: what did you try, what changed, what evidence, what remains?
If the action has not started, identify the reason and the next realistic step.
Distinguish completion from effect: sent for approval, approved, and usable are different stages.

keyPoints.chapter: Reflect and choose your next step
points: Three optional questions: what do you understand more clearly, what matters most for people affected, what will you do next?
The companion sheet gathers purpose, barrier, standards, change, authority, participation, assistance, evidence, concern route and follow-up.
It is a personal working copy, not an official record or an approval.
Return to any lesson or the original standards when a new situation arises.
Current policy, specialist guidance and people's experience still matter; the curriculum supports judgment, it does not replace requirements.
A next step does not have to be large: a clearer question, a more usable instruction, an appropriate escalation.

sections.heading: Plan
items: Issue, written as an observation.
Intended experience: understand the purpose, consider choices, request assistance, respond.
Proposed change and the standards it connects to.
Action, responsible role, resources, review point.
What remains uncertain, and the next inquiry for each.

sections.heading: Check
items: Begins with inquiry? Preserves the person's choices?
Usable assistance route? Within the appropriate authority?
People affected involved? Credible way to check the result?
Any new barrier: a lost route, lost information, a decision already closed?

sections.heading: Follow up (about 30 days)
items: What did you try? What changed? What evidence? What remains?
If not started: why, and what is the next realistic step?
Sent for approval, approved, and usable are different stages; say which you reached.

remember: Keep official records in approved systems; the companion sheet is a personal working copy.
A clearer question or a more usable instruction is a worthwhile next step.
askWho: Your supervisor or an appropriate colleague, for a non-sensitive summary at follow-up.
The original standards and current policy, when a new situation arises.
